name: Theobromine
lead: Theobromine is the main alkaloid of the cacao plant (Theobroma cacao) and a dimethylxanthine closely related to caffeine and theophylline. It occurs in cocoa and chocolate, with smaller amounts in tea, yerba mate, kola nut and guarana.[1][2] Reference works describe it as a mild diuretic, heart stimulant and bronchodilator with much weaker central nervous system stimulation than caffeine.[1]

In appearance-oriented discussion it is grouped with de-puffing and water-balance compounds because of its diuretic classification, the chain being a mild diuretic effect, less retained fluid and a leaner-looking face. Others mention it as a gentler stimulant in pre-workout and focus blends, the chain being steadier energy, better training and a better physique.[18] No published study has tested whether theobromine reduces facial puffiness or otherwise changes appearance; the human trials that exist examined mood, cognition, blood pressure, lipids, cough and dental outcomes.[3][4]

Because the amount in dietary chocolate is small and the compound is sold as a food ingredient and supplement in many places, it is not a prescription product in most jurisdictions; in South Korea it has been sold as a prescription cough ingredient.[1] Wikipedia also notes industrial use as a food additive and as a precursor for some cosmetics.[1]
infobox: Cacao beans; also tea, kola, guarana, yerba mate[1]

paras: Theobromine is a flat, slightly water-soluble purine derivative that differs from caffeine by lacking one methyl group. The name derives from the Greek words for god and food and does not refer to bromine [1]. It is the principal alkaloid in cacao, at roughly 1.5 to 3 percent of the dry bean, with dark chocolate generally containing more than milk chocolate and cocoa powder the most concentrated common food source [1][2]. Commercially it is extracted from cocoa husks left over from chocolate production [2].

Cocoa beans contain about 1 percent theobromine according to Wikipedia, and a 28 g serving of milk chocolate has about 60 mg versus about 200 mg for dark chocolate.[1] Mean concentrations per 100 g are listed as 2,060 mg in cocoa powder, 266 mg in cocoa beverages, 195 mg in chocolate toppings, 147 mg in chocolate bakery products and 22.6 mg in chocolate milk.[1] Other sources include tea, yaupon and guayusa hollies, yerba mate and kola nut, and guarana in trace amounts.[1] Caffeine is metabolised in the liver partly to theobromine, along with paraxanthine and theophylline.[1][5]

Forum users on T Nation discuss theobromine as the compound behind chocolate's mild stimulant effect, describing it as a weaker relative of caffeine.[16] Another T Nation thread, on caffeine alternatives, notes that coffee contains theophylline and theobromine as well as caffeine, and users list theobromine among ingredients in pre-workout formulas.[17][18] The de-puffing idea, applying the mild diuretic classification to the face, is a reasoning from pharmacology rather than a result from trials; no appearance outcomes have been studied.[1]

Wikipedia describes theobromine as a mild heart stimulant, diuretic and bronchodilator that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, and notes it is sold in South Korea as a 300 mg prescription cough product.[1] A registered trial examined a theobromine capsule as an antitussive in 332 people with acute bronchitis, and registered studies have tested theobromine toothpaste for dentin hypersensitivity and plaque.[8][9][10] Industrially it is a food additive and a precursor for some cosmetics.[1]

Theobromine blocks adenosine receptors and is a weaker phosphodiesterase inhibitor than other methylxanthines [1]. It is more lipid-soluble than caffeine and reaches peak blood levels more slowly, about two to three hours after ingestion, and is metabolised in the liver by CYP1A2 and CYP2E1 enzymes [1][5]. Its elimination half-life is reported as about 6 to 9 hours [1][2]. It is classed among diuretics in the ATC system [1].

A psychopharmacology study in healthy volunteers examined theobromine's effects directly.[11] Wikipedia says the central stimulant effect is not significant, and that limited mood effects appeared at around 250 mg per day.[1]

Intakes of roughly 0.8 to 1.5 grams per day have been reported to cause sweating, trembling and severe headache [1]. Theobromine is the main reason chocolate is toxic to dogs and cats, which clear it slowly [1][2].

Wikipedia notes that theobromine may contribute to heartburn by affecting the lower esophageal sphincter.[1] For dogs, the median lethal dose is reported as 100 to 200 mg per kilogram, and dark chocolate, with roughly 10 g/kg theobromine, is far more dangerous per weight than milk chocolate at 1 to 5 g/kg; symptoms include digestive upset, excitability, slow heart rate and later seizures.[1] The IARC has published a monograph on theobromine's evaluation as a possible carcinogen.[12]

Registered human studies of theobromine have examined acute physiological effects of different serving regimens [3], mood, cognition and blood pressure compared with caffeine [4], blood lipid parameters in 152 healthy subjects [6], vascular function and intestinal apoA-I production [7], and an antitussive capsule in 332 people with acute bronchitis [8]. Others have looked at theobromine toothpaste and dentin hypersensitivity [9][10]. Results are mixed and often confounded when studied as part of cocoa, where flavanols also contribute [2]. No study found has examined theobromine for facial puffiness, water retention or other appearance outcomes.

A 2025 paper in Aging reported that theobromine is associated with slower epigenetic ageing.[13] Cocoa flavanol trials, which are distinct from theobromine, include an 8-day crossover in 11 healthy adults that used caffeine- and theobromine-matched placebo and found no effect of 900 mg/day flavanols on cold-induced vasodilation, and a nutritional intervention on cutaneous photoprotection with high-flavanol cocoa.[14][15] Because cocoa contains both flavanols and theobromine, effects seen with cocoa are not attributable to theobromine alone.[2]

Theobromine is best known to the public as the reason chocolate is dangerous for dogs and cats, which clear it slowly.[1] In supplement culture it shows up as a minor ingredient in pre-workout stacks and is mentioned in discussions of caffeine alternatives.[17][18] The name, from Greek roots for food of the gods, does not refer to bromine.[1]

card.summary: Cocoa's main xanthine, a mild diuretic with no published evidence for de-puffing.
card.note: Diuretic classification is not backed by appearance studies.

quick.overview:
Theobromine is the main stimulant-like compound in cocoa. It is chemically close to caffeine but acts more weakly on the nervous system.

It is grouped with depuffing compounds because reference works call it a mild diuretic. No study has tested it for facial puffiness or other appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: It blocks adenosine receptors and weakly inhibits phosphodiesterases, with effects on blood vessels, heart and kidneys described in reference works. It is metabolised by liver CYP1A2 and CYP2E1 with a half-life of about 6 to 9 hours.
quick.risks: Reported effects at high intakes include sweating, tremor and headache. It is notably toxic to dogs and cats. Regulatory status is as a food ingredient in most places.

chain: Dietary theobromine from cocoa or a supplement
Possible loss of some retained water
angle.text: People who talk about theobromine in appearance terms are mostly thinking about its mild diuretic classification and its place in cocoa, which is also associated with flavanol research on skin. It is also used as a gentler stimulant alongside caffeine in training supplements.
